Reliable Remote Inference
from Unreliable Components:
Joint Communication and Computation Limits

Zhenyu Liu    Yi Ma    Rahim Tafazolli ††thanks: Z. Liu, Y. Ma, and R. Tafazolli are with the 6GIC, Institute for Communication Systems, University of Surrey, Guildford, United Kingdom, GU2 7XH (e-mail: {zhenyu.liu, y.ma, r.tafazolli}@surrey.ac.uk).
Abstract

Classical information theory typically assumes reliable receiver-side processing. We study remote inference when communication is noisy and the receiver itself is built from unreliable components under a finite redundancy budget. Under a committed/no-bypass receiver closure, task-relevant information can affect the final estimate only by passing through a budgeted collection of vulnerable primitives unless an explicit protected bypass is modeled. Modeling each vulnerable primitive as a memoryless noisy channel yields a baseline supply–demand converse: the task-relevant information needed to attain a target distortion cannot exceed the smaller of the total information supplied by the communication channel and the total information supplied by the vulnerable compute budget. Our main converse shows that committed intermediate interfaces create additional first-order serial cuts and receiver-internal computation-graph cuts, captured in general by a receiver-internal compute min-cut converse. In particular, the twofold loss in the symmetric two-stage hard-separation special case is not inherent to unreliable receiver computation but induced by hard-separation under the committed/no-bypass closure. This extra first-order tax is therefore closure-dependent rather than universal. On the converse side, if downstream modules retain soft visibility to the raw channel output, the converse reduces to the single-bottleneck supply, up to any explicitly reserved soft-path budget. Under a separate stronger protected-support closure with reliable decoder and control support, we establish achievability results for task-direct and serial hard-separation constructions. For the fully noisy-logic regime, we obtain only a conservative depth-dependent converse, and matched achievability remains open.

Index Terms: 
Remote inference, indirect rate–distortion, unreliable receiver computation, hard-separation.

I Introduction

Classical information theory [1] typically treats receiver-side decoding and downstream processing as reliable. This paper studies when remote inference remains possible with noisy communication and an unreliable receiver under a finite redundancy budget. That classical abstraction is increasingly strained in two distinct but converging regimes. First, energy-driven hardware trends such as near-threshold voltage operation and approximate computing can introduce timing violations, transient faults, and stochastic bit flips within the receiver pipeline [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Second, harsh-environment deployments such as in-orbit inference can induce radiation-driven soft errors that corrupt accelerator state in addition to channel noise. Recent measurement and emulation studies report SEU-style single-bit flips and spatially correlated multi-bit upsets (MCUs) in accelerator memories and radiation-prone inference settings [7, 8]. Complementary systems work develops software protection mechanisms that convert many silent corruptions into detected failures or erasures on practical accelerators [9, 10]. In such regimes, the reliability of remote inference is no longer governed by the channel alone, but by a three-way tradeoff among (i) channel resources, (ii) compute resources, and (iii) the end task (e.g., estimation or inference) that consumes the received information.

The missing benchmark

Information-theoretic treatments of unreliable communication and unreliable computation have largely evolved along separate tracks. The noisy computation literature asks how to compute reliably using faulty components [11, 12, 13, 14], while the communication literature asks how to convey information reliably over noisy channels. Neither directly answers the task-centric question here: what joint communication and compute budget (equivalently, redundancy budget) is required to achieve a target task level (e.g., a distortion threshold or a distortion tail) despite receiver-side unreliability? We address this through a supply–demand lens: the demand is task-relevant information (captured by indirect/remote rate–distortion), and the supply is jointly bottlenecked by channel capacity and a compute information budget.

Problem setup and questions

We consider remote inference where an encoder observes YY correlated with a latent source XX and the receiver produces X^\hat{X} under a distortion constraint. Communication uses a discrete memoryless channel of capacity CchC_{\mathrm{ch}} for nn channel uses per source sample. Receiver-side processing is performed on an unreliable digital substrate with a budget of mm noisy primitives per sample. We model each primitive as a discrete memoryless channel with per-use capacity CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}} (a canonical baseline is a binary symmetric channel (BSC) with crossover probability ε\varepsilon, so Cgate=1−h2​(ε)C_{\mathrm{gate}}=1-h_{2}\!\left(\varepsilon\right)), so that the receiver has an aggregate compute information supply of m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}} bits per sample (Definition II.1). Within this model we ask: (i) what task distortion levels are fundamentally achievable under joint communication and computation constraints? (ii) when decoding itself is noisy, does enforcing a hard digital interface between “decoding” and “task computation” impose additional unavoidable penalties compared to task-direct processing?

Scope clarification

The additional first-order penalty studied here is not a universal consequence of receiver noise. It appears when task-relevant information must cross committed vulnerable interfaces that remove downstream access to the raw channel output. When downstream modules retain access to Rn​TR^{nT} within the committed/no-bypass closure, the converse reduces to the single-bottleneck supply. An explicit protected side path relaxes the active cut, but if a committed vulnerable interface remains, residual serial cuts may still persist; see Definition II.6, Propositions IV.19 and IV.20, and Corollaries III.6 and IV.14.

I-A Related Work and Positioning

Noisy computation: from circuit complexity to information supply

Noisy computation has a long history, from von Neumann’s seminal work on reliable computation from unreliable components [11] to information-decay and redundancy lower bounds for noisy circuits [12, 15, 13]. Complementing circuit-level viewpoints, Simon [14] introduced information-theoretic notions of computation capacity for noisy function evaluation. Those works primarily study reliable computation of a specified function. Here the objective is instead task-centric: approximate reconstruction under a distortion criterion, with receiver computation coupled to communication through an explicit per-instance budget mm.

Faulty decoding: algorithm-specific analyses vs. algorithm-agnostic converses

Computation noise inside iterative decoders has been studied extensively, for example for low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoding under faulty updates [16] and belief propagation on noisy hardware [17]. Those are algorithm-specific bit-recovery analyses. Our results are complementary: they give algorithm-agnostic, task-centric converses and corresponding achievability statements under an explicit compute budget, with the converse side upper bounding the task-relevant mutual information deliverable by any receiver algorithm. In particular, Theorem IV.2 shows that when decoding and task execution share the same unreliable substrate, a committed hard interface creates an additional first-order bottleneck. Unlike classical source–channel separation, where an intermediate digital description does not create a new first-order bottleneck below channel capacity [1, 18], a committed interface here must itself be materialized and re-consumed through noisy primitives, so task-relevant information crosses two serial compute cuts.

Indirect rate–distortion and task-oriented communication

The indirect (remote) rate–distortion problem [19, 20] characterizes the mutual-information demand needed to reconstruct XX from an observation YY under a distortion constraint. More broadly, task-oriented or semantic communication formulations optimize task performance rather than signal reconstruction [21, 22]. These models typically assume reliable receiver-side processing. Our contribution is to make receiver computation noise and a compute budget explicit first-order information bottlenecks and to show that they can change both the task limit and the validity of hard-separation.

Additional-noise and noisy-receiver models

Receiver-side impairments have also been studied directly in classical information theory, including additional-noise models [23], source encoding from a randomly disturbed observation [24], and minimum-distortion transmission to a noisy receiver [25]. Those formulations typically append a noisy observation or reproduction map to an otherwise reliable receiver. Our bottleneck is different in kind: it is induced by receiver-internal committed materialization and re-consumption under an explicit compute budget. At a formal level, Theorem IV.9 is cut-set-like, but it should not be read as a classical communication-network cut-set with exogenous link capacities: the cut edges are receiver-internal committed interfaces whose capacities are induced compute-supply limits, and the demand side is indirect rate–distortion rather than reliable message throughput; see Remark IV.3.

System motivation and finite-blocklength context

Practical fault mechanisms motivate the abstraction, but the main theorems depend on the substrate only through information-supply parameters such as m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}} or ∑iCi\sum_{i}C_{i} and, for tail benchmarks, coarse undetected-error/detected-erasure (UE–ER) parameters; see Subsection F-C. Classical finite-blocklength lossy joint source–channel coding (JSCC) shows that with reliable receiver-side processing, separation incurs only a dispersion-level penalty at short blocklengths/latencies [26]. By contrast, the committed-interface penalty studied here is a first-order compute-supply loss caused by serial vulnerable cuts, and it persists in Shannon asymptotics.

I-B Contributions

Task demand is quantified by the indirect (remote) rate–distortion function RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D). Unless explicitly stated otherwise, the baseline and serial-interface converse results below are stated under the committed/no-bypass closure. All achievability statements in this subsection are instead under the stronger protected-support closure of Assumption III.7; they should not be read as a matched characterization under a single common closure.

Baseline supply–demand converse

For task-direct processing, Theorem III.5 proves

RX|Y​(D)≤min⁡{n​Cch,m​Cgate},R_{X|Y}(D)\leq\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\;mC_{\mathrm{gate}}\}, (1)

which serves as the paper’s baseline supply–demand converse. It isolates the two basic first-order supplies: the physical-channel supply n​CchnC_{\mathrm{ch}} and the vulnerable-compute supply m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}}. Corollary III.6 shows how an explicit protected side path of rate bb bits per task instance relaxes the task-direct compute cut to b+m​Cgateb+mC_{\mathrm{gate}}. Under Assumption III.7, Theorem III.8 gives the task-direct achievability result, while Theorem IV.15 gives the protected-bypass achievability theorem for the two-stage architecture.

Architecture theorem chain

The main architectural point is that, once remote inference is implemented through committed vulnerable interfaces, the first-order converse depends on receiver architecture. Theorem IV.9 gives the master receiver-internal compute min-cut converse

RX|Y(D)≤min{nCch,minΩ:s𝒢∈Ω,t𝒢∉Ω∑e∈∂+(Ω)meCgate},R_{X|Y}(D)\leq\min\Big\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\;\min_{\Omega:\,s_{\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega,\,t_{\mathcal{G}}\notin\Omega}\sum_{e\in\partial^{+}(\Omega)}m_{e}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\Big\}, (2)

Equation (2) should therefore be interpreted under the committed/no-bypass closure: its cut values are induced compute-supply limits, not exogenous communication-link capacities. Theorems IV.2 and IV.5 are its two-stage and KK-stage serial specializations. In particular, the familiar twofold hard-separation loss is not inherent to unreliable receiver computation; it arises only in the symmetric two-stage hard-separation special case of this more general receiver-internal compute-cut phenomenon. Proposition IV.19 shows, on the converse side, that if downstream modules retain soft visibility to the raw channel output within that closure, the converse reduces to the single-bottleneck supply, up to any explicitly reserved soft-path budget; see also Proposition IV.20. Theorem IV.4 and Corollary IV.6 give the corresponding serial achievability results.

Variants and separate noisy-logic closure

Protected bypasses, reliable islands, soft interfaces, and heterogeneous primitive capacities enter by modifying the active cut or its effective capacity, yielding a unified picture of when the hard-separation penalty is relaxed, eliminated, or replaced by another bottleneck; the protected-bypass and reliable-island cases also receive achievability results. Section V then studies a stricter closure in which the entire receiver logic, including control and bookkeeping, is noisy. In that regime, Theorem V.3 gives a conservative depth-dependent converse through the effective per-gate supply Clogic​(dlogic,δ,Kfan)C_{\mathrm{logic}}(d_{\mathrm{logic}},\delta,K_{\mathrm{fan}}) defined in (84); a matched achievability characterization remains open.

I-C Paper Outline

Sections II–III formalize the committed/no-bypass model, the task-demand notion, and the reference supply plane. Section IV develops the receiver-internal cut converses, their serial specializations, and the main architectural variants. Section V studies the separate noisy-logic closure. Section VI gives compact discrete and scalar-Gaussian examples. The appendices collect finite-blocklength and tail benchmarks, UE–ER refinements, throughput mappings, and supplementary variants and extensions.

II Model and Architectural Taxonomy

This section fixes the baseline committed/no-bypass receiver model, the task-demand notion, and the architectural taxonomy used by the converse results. The emphasis is on which information paths are permitted to reach the task output, while finite-TT tail criteria and benchmark refinements are deferred to Appendix A.

II-A Notation and Conventions

We index task instances (samples) within a coding block by t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\dots,T\}, where TT is the task-blocklength (the number of task instances coded jointly). We denote length-TT task blocks by superscripts, e.g., XT=(X1,…,XT)X^{T}=(X_{1},\dots,X_{T}) and YT=(Y1,…,YT)Y^{T}=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{T}). For each task instance tt, the transmitter uses nn physical channel uses, producing channel input/output vectors StnS_{t}^{n} and RtnR_{t}^{n}. Over a task block of length TT, the physical channel is therefore used Nch≜n​TN_{\mathrm{ch}}\triangleq nT times (we often write sequences as Sn​TS^{nT} and Rn​TR^{nT} to keep the dependence on (n,T)(n,T) explicit). Likewise, the receiver is allowed at most mm uses of an unreliable binary primitive per task instance (Definition II.1), i.e., at most L≜m​TL\triangleq mT primitive uses per task block; in hard-separation this budget is allocated across decoding and downstream task inference with mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m.

Here tt indexes task instances rather than physical seconds; individual physical channel uses within a block are indexed by ℓ∈{1,…,n​T}\ell\in\{1,\dots,nT\} (equivalently ℓ∈{1,…,Nch}\ell\in\{1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{ch}}\}), unreliable primitive uses by ii, and serial stages by kk. Physical time re-enters only when mapping per-second budgets or hardware error rates into per-instance parameters, e.g., via the throughput λ\lambda in Appendix D or via a dwell time τ\tau in a soft-error-rate mapping.

We reserve the superscript T for length-TT task blocks (sequences). If matrix/vector transposes appear (e.g., in linear-Gaussian extensions), we denote transpose by (⋅)⊤(\cdot)^{\top} (or (⋅)𝖳(\cdot)^{\mathsf{T}}) to avoid overloading T.

We use ε∈[0,12)\varepsilon\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}) for the BSC crossover probability of the unreliable compute primitive, while ϵ\epsilon (with subscripts) denotes reliability targets such as excess-distortion probabilities and block error probabilities in finite-blocklength benchmarks. The physical channel capacity is denoted by CchC_{\mathrm{ch}} (bits/use) and the primitive “compute capacity” by CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}} (bits/primitive use); the canonical BSC(ε)(\varepsilon) specialization is introduced in Subsection II-E. Unless otherwise noted, mutual information and rate quantities are measured in bits (base-2 logarithms), and “bits/sample” means per task instance. Table I summarizes the frequently used symbols and conventions for reference.

II-B Source, Observation, and Task Distortion

At each task instance indexed by tt, a latent variable XtX_{t} is observed through YtY_{t} with a known joint law PX,YP_{X,Y}. The receiver produces an estimate X^t\hat{X}_{t} and incurs a single-letter distortion d⁡(Xt,X^t)d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t}). We focus on average distortion

D≜𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)].D\triangleq\mathbb{E}\big[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})\big]. (3)

The mean-distortion criterion above is the primary first-order task metric for the core converse chain. Tail/excess-distortion criteria and finite-TT refinements are deferred to Appendix A.

II-C Channel Model and Per-Instance Communication Budget

Per task instance, the communication budget is nn channel uses. For the formal information-theoretic statements below, the encoder may be stochastic and may map an entire observation block YTY^{T} to Sn​TS^{nT}; the single-instance picture Yt↦StnY_{t}\mapsto S_{t}^{n} is recovered when T=1T=1. The channel is memoryless with transition law PR|SP_{R|S} (e.g., additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN)) and a standard input constraint (e.g., average power). Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the set of admissible input distributions under this constraint. The per-use capacity is

Cch≜supPS∈𝒫I⁡(S,R).C_{\mathrm{ch}}\triangleq\sup_{P_{S}\in\mathcal{P}}I(S;R). (4)

Thus, the physical channel can supply at most n​CchnC_{\mathrm{ch}} bits of mutual information per task instance, or equivalently n​T​CchnTC_{\mathrm{ch}} bits over a task block of length TT.

II-D Blocklength-TT Formulation and Standing Assumptions

For information-theoretic statements (converse and achievability), it is useful to consider a block of TT task instances. Let (XT,YT)={(Xt,Yt)}t=1T(X^{T},Y^{T})=\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} denote the source–observation pairs. Unless otherwise stated, we adopt the following standing assumptions (S1)–(S3).

  • •

    (S1) Memorylessness across task instances: (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) are i.i.d. according to PX,YP_{X,Y}.

  • •

    (S2) Memoryless channel: conditioned on inputs Sn​TS^{nT}, the channel outputs satisfy PRn​T|Sn​T=∏ℓ=1n​TPR|SP_{R^{nT}|S^{nT}}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{nT}P_{R|S}.

  • •

    (S3) Per-instance resource budgets: the encoder uses nn channel uses per task instance, so the block uses Nch≜n​TN_{\mathrm{ch}}\triangleq nT channel uses in total. The receiver is allowed at most mm unreliable primitives per task instance, i.e., at most L≜m​TL\triangleq mT unreliable primitives in the block.

The receiver may be stochastic and interacts with the noisy-computation substrate (Definition II.1) for at most L=m​TL=mT unreliable primitives before outputting an estimate X^T\hat{X}^{T}. The average distortion constraint is

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\big[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})\big]\leq D. (5)

The per-instance budgets (n,m)(n,m) are the natural objects once communication bandwidth and compute energy/latency scale linearly with throughput; Appendix D makes this explicit by translating per-second budgets into per-instance budgets via the sampling rate λ\lambda.

II-E Unreliable Computation Substrate and Per-Instance Compute Budget

We model receiver-side processing as an interactive algorithm that, in order to persist intermediate digital state, must repeatedly commit values to vulnerable storage (or other unreliable primitives) and later retrieve/use them. Each such vulnerable materialization is abstracted as one use of a discrete memoryless channel (DMC) WZ|UW_{Z|U} from an intended input UU to an available output ZZ. The corresponding per-use compute information supply is the Shannon capacity

Cgate≜maxPU⁡I⁡(U,Z)bits/primitive.C_{\mathrm{gate}}\triangleq\max_{P_{U}}I(U;Z)\quad\text{bits/primitive}. (6)

Canonical baseline: BSC(ε)(\varepsilon) (independent bit flips)

A canonical and analytically convenient specialization is BSC(ε)(\varepsilon), which models independent bit flips during a store--retrieve (materialization) operation.11 1 We adopt an i.i.d. BSC(ε)(\varepsilon) bit-flip model as an analytically convenient baseline. Architecture-level resilience studies commonly abstract transient faults as random bit corruptions, often implemented as randomly selected single-bit flips in architectural state; see, e.g., [27, 28, 29, 30].

In this baseline, each vulnerable bit materialization is modeled as

Z=U⊕N,N∼Bern⁡(ε),0≤ε<12,Z=U\oplus N,\qquad N\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon),\quad 0\leq\varepsilon<\tfrac{1}{2}, (7)

where UU is the intended stored bit and ZZ is the bit value subsequently available to the algorithm after potential flips. The per-bit information capacity of this bit-flip mechanism is

Cgate≜1−h2​(ε)bits/primitive,C_{\mathrm{gate}}\triangleq 1-h_{2}\!\left(\varepsilon\right)\quad\text{bits/primitive}, (8)

where h2​(p)≜−p​log2​p−(1−p)​log2⁡(1−p)h_{2}(p)\triangleq-p\log_{2}p-(1-p)\log_{2}(1-p) denotes the binary entropy function (base-2).

All converses in this paper depend on the compute substrate only through an upper bound on the per-use mutual information that can cross each vulnerable primitive use. Therefore, the results extend directly to any DMC WZ|UW_{Z|U} by plugging in an appropriate effective CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}} (or, under heterogeneity, a sum of class-dependent supplies as in Lemma F.1); Subsection F-C records the corresponding plug-in and calibration view.

We measure receiver compute/energy/latency constraints via a bit-materialization budget: per task instance, the receiver may cause at most mm such vulnerable bit materializations. If the graphics processing unit (GPU) operates on ww-bit words, then one word-level store corresponds to ww parallel bit materializations; throughout, mm counts bits rather than words.

To make the compute bottleneck information-theoretically explicit, we adopt the following interactive model.

Definition II.1 (Committed/no-bypass noisy-materialization receiver model).

Given the channel output RtnR_{t}^{n}, a (possibly randomized) receiver algorithm interacts with an unreliable digital substrate (e.g., a GPU/accelerator) whose intermediate stored bits—including both task-dependent intermediates (e.g., activations/messages) and task-independent parameters (e.g., quantized deep neural network (DNN) weights) when stored in vulnerable memory—are subject to independent flips. At materialization i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}, the algorithm selects an intermediate bit UiU_{i} as a (measurable) function of (Rtn,Zi−1)(R_{t}^{n},Z^{i-1}) and stores it in a vulnerable state element. The value that is later available to subsequent computation is Zi=Ui⊕NiZ_{i}=U_{i}\oplus N_{i} with Ni∼i.i.d.Bern⁡(ε)N_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon). After mm materializations, the final task output satisfies X^t=g⁡(Zm)\hat{X}_{t}=g(Z^{m}) for some measurable function gg. Thus any task-relevant information from RtnR_{t}^{n} that influences X^t\hat{X}_{t} must be committed to vulnerable state at least once and traverse a noisy primitive. Adaptive access to RtnR_{t}^{n} when choosing the materializations is allowed, but no additional reliable path from RtnR_{t}^{n} to X^t\hat{X}_{t} is present unless it is modeled explicitly through a protected bypass or related extension.

Remark II.2 (Why commitment matters).

This theorem-bearing information-structure assumption still permits fully adaptive read–compute–store strategies; it is precisely what turns Lemma III.1 into a genuine compute cut.

Remark II.3 (bb-bit reliable bypass / accounting).

Some receiver implementations retain a protected path from the raw channel output to the final task output [9, 10]. We model this by an auxiliary variable VtV_{t} satisfying H⁡(Vt)≤bH(V_{t})\leq b bits and X^t=g⁡(Zm,Vt)\hat{X}_{t}=g(Z^{m},V_{t}), so the bypass contributes a reliable side path of rate bb bits/sample. Protected output-relevant artifacts are charged to bb, whereas vulnerable materializations count toward mm. Resident or reliably stored weights contribute little or no per-instance budget, whereas weights re-materialized through vulnerable memory on each inference must be charged to mm. Detailed accelerator-specific mappings, including weight loading and the learned-inference proxy in (205), are deferred to Appendix I.

Figure 1 summarizes this protected-bypass versus vulnerable-materialization accounting.

II-F Task Demand: Indirect (Remote) Rate–Distortion

The task demand for achieving distortion DD is quantified by the indirect rate–distortion function [19, 20]

RX|Y(D)≜infPX^|Y:𝔼⁡[d⁡(X,X^)]≤DI(Y;X^).R_{X|Y}(D)\triangleq\inf_{P_{\hat{X}|Y}:\ \mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat{X})]\leq D}I(Y;\hat{X}). (9)
Remark II.4 (Induced-distortion view).

Define the induced distortion d¯​(y,x^)≜𝔼⁡[d⁡(X,x^)∣Y=y]\bar{d}(y,\hat{x})\triangleq\mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat{x})\mid Y=y]. Then 𝔼⁡[d⁡(X,X^)]≤D\mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat{X})]\leq D is equivalent to 𝔼​[d¯​(Y,X^)]≤D\mathbb{E}[\bar{d}(Y,\hat{X})]\leq D, and hence RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D) is the (direct) rate–distortion function of source YY under distortion measure d¯\bar{d}; see Lemma A.3. This viewpoint is reused for the finite-blocklength/dispersion refinements in Appendix A.

Proposition II.5 (Operational indirect rate–distortion theorem).

For the memoryless block model introduced in Subsection II-D, and under the standard regularity conditions for rate–distortion theory, RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D) equals the minimum asymptotically achievable fixed-length rate for reproducing XTX^{T} from YTY^{T} under average distortion DD. Equivalently, for every R>RX|Y​(D)R>R_{X|Y}(D) there exist fixed-length codes (fT,ψT)(f_{T},\psi_{T}) with |𝒲T|≤2T​R|\mathcal{W}_{T}|\leq 2^{TR} and

X^T=ψT​(fT​(YT)),lim supT→∞1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D,\hat{X}^{T}=\psi_{T}(f_{T}(Y^{T})),\qquad\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})]\leq D,

while any such sequence must satisfy R≥RX|Y​(D)R\geq R_{X|Y}(D).

Proof.

By Lemma A.3, RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D) is exactly the ordinary rate–distortion function of the source YY under the induced distortion measure d¯\bar{d}. The claim therefore follows from Shannon’s classical fixed-length lossy source coding theorem applied to the memoryless source YTY^{T} under distortion d¯\bar{d}; see, e.g., [19, 18]. ∎

II-G Two Receiver Architectures

We distinguish two baseline receiver organizations: Architecture (A) is a task-direct receiver and Architecture (B) is a hard-separation receiver. Soft-interface relaxations are formalized after the baseline hard-separation model.

Task-direct processing

The receiver maps the channel output directly to X^t\hat{X}_{t} using the full compute budget of mm noisy bit materializations:

Yt→EncStn→channelRtn→m noisy bit materializationstask-directX^t.Y_{t}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Enc}}S_{t}^{n}\xrightarrow{\text{channel}}R_{t}^{n}\xrightarrow[\text{$m$ noisy bit materializations}]{\text{task-direct}}\hat{X}_{t}. (10)

Hard-separation with an intermediate digital interface

The receiver first forms an intermediate digital representation B^t\hat{B}_{t} and then performs task computation using only B^t\hat{B}_{t} as input:

Yt→EncStn→channelRtn→mdec noisy bit materializationsnoisy decodeB^t→mtask noisy bit materializationsnoisy taskX^t,mdec+mtask≤m.Y_{t}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Enc}}S_{t}^{n}\xrightarrow{\text{channel}}R_{t}^{n}\xrightarrow[\text{$m_{\mathrm{dec}}$ noisy bit materializations}]{\text{noisy decode}}\hat{B}_{t}\xrightarrow[\text{$m_{\mathrm{task}}$ noisy bit materializations}]{\text{noisy task}}\hat{X}_{t},\qquad m_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m. (11)

This downstream-visibility constraint is formalized in Definition II.6.

Definition II.6 (Hard-separation with a committed digital interface).

A TT-block receiver architecture satisfies hard-separation if there exists an intermediate digital interface random variable B^T\hat{B}^{T} (taking values in a finite alphabet, e.g., {0,1}Lif​T\{0,1\}^{L_{\mathrm{if}}T} for some interface length LifL_{\mathrm{if}}) such that the induced joint law obeys the Markov chain YT→Sn​T→Rn​T→B^T→X^TY^{T}\to S^{nT}\to R^{nT}\to\hat{B}^{T}\to\hat{X}^{T}, and such that (i) B^T\hat{B}^{T} is computed from Rn​TR^{nT} on the noisy-computation substrate using at most mdec​Tm_{\mathrm{dec}}T vulnerable primitive uses, (ii) X^T\hat{X}^{T} is computed from B^T\hat{B}^{T} (and not from Rn​TR^{nT}) on the same substrate using at most mtask​Tm_{\mathrm{task}}T primitive uses, with mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m. If the downstream stage retains access to Rn​TR^{nT} or protected side information derived from it in addition to B^T\hat{B}^{T}, the architecture becomes a soft-interface relaxation and leaves pure hard-separation. In that case the extra serial tax studied below is no longer mandatory; see Proposition IV.19, Proposition IV.20, and Corollary III.6. The hard/soft qualifier refers to downstream information visibility, not to whether B^T\hat{B}^{T} itself contains multi-bit “soft” statistics. If the task stage observes only B^T\hat{B}^{T}, the Markov chain still holds and the serial hard-separation converse continues to apply.

Figure 2 summarizes both organizations, while Table II places them in the broader architecture/closure taxonomy used later.

III Baseline Reference Bound and Achievability Under a Protected-Support Closure

This section records the baseline reference bound for the committed/no-bypass closure and the corresponding achievability result under Assumption III.7.

III-A A Per-Instance Compute Information Bound

Our converses rely on a single abstract “compute cut”: each time the receiver commits information to a vulnerable primitive, at most CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}} bits of mutual information can cross that primitive use, even under adaptive operation. Thus any module using at most mm such primitives can convey at most m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}} bits from its input to its final output. We first state this principle in a general conditional-capacity form and then record the baseline bit-flip specialization together with the reliable-bypass plug-in used later. Additional heterogeneous and word-level plug-ins are deferred to Appendix F.

Lemma III.1 (General compute information bound under a conditional-capacity constraint).

Consider an interactive receiver module that observes an input UU and uses mm unreliable primitives sequentially. At use ii, it selects an intended primitive input UiU_{i} as a (possibly randomized) function of (U,Zi−1)(U,Z^{i-1}) and then obtains an output ZiZ_{i} according to some conditional law PZi|Ui,Zi−1(⋅∣⋅,zi−1)P_{Z_{i}|U_{i},Z^{i-1}}(\cdot\mid\cdot,z^{i-1}). Assume that, for every history zi−1z^{i-1}, the induced conditional channel has capacity at most CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}}, i.e.,

maxPUi⁡I⁡(Ui;Zi∣Zi−1=zi−1)≤Cgate.\max_{P_{U_{i}}}I(U_{i};Z_{i}\mid Z^{i-1}=z^{i-1})\leq C_{\mathrm{gate}}. (12)

Then the module output U^=g⁡(Zm)\hat{U}=g(Z^{m}) satisfies

I⁡(U,U^)≤I⁡(U,Zm)≤m​Cgate.I(U;\hat{U})\leq I(U;Z^{m})\leq m\,C_{\mathrm{gate}}. (13)
Proof.

By data processing, I⁡(U,U^)≤I⁡(U,Zm)I(U;\hat{U})\leq I(U;Z^{m}) since U^=g⁡(Zm)\hat{U}=g(Z^{m}). For the second inequality, apply the chain rule:

I⁡(U,Zm)=∑i=1mI⁡(U;Zi∣Zi−1).I(U;Z^{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}I(U;Z_{i}\mid Z^{i-1}). (14)

Fix ii and condition on Zi−1=zi−1Z^{i-1}=z^{i-1}. By construction, the intended primitive input UiU_{i} is generated as a (possibly randomized) function of (U,zi−1)(U,z^{i-1}). Moreover, the primitive output ZiZ_{i} is drawn according to the conditional law PZi|Ui,Zi−1(⋅∣⋅,zi−1)P_{Z_{i}|U_{i},Z^{i-1}}(\cdot\mid\cdot,z^{i-1}), which depends on UU only through UiU_{i}. Equivalently,

PZi|U,Ui,Zi−1(⋅∣u,ui,zi−1)=PZi|Ui,Zi−1(⋅∣ui,zi−1),P_{Z_{i}|U,U_{i},Z^{i-1}}(\cdot\mid u,u_{i},z^{i-1})=P_{Z_{i}|U_{i},Z^{i-1}}(\cdot\mid u_{i},z^{i-1}),

so U→Ui→ZiU\to U_{i}\to Z_{i} forms a Markov chain conditional on Zi−1=zi−1Z^{i-1}=z^{i-1}. Hence

I⁡(U;Zi∣Zi−1=zi−1)≤I⁡(Ui;Zi∣Zi−1=zi−1)≤CgateI(U;Z_{i}\mid Z^{i-1}=z^{i-1})\leq I(U_{i};Z_{i}\mid Z^{i-1}=z^{i-1})\leq C_{\mathrm{gate}} (15)

by (12). Averaging over Zi−1Z^{i-1} yields I⁡(U;Zi∣Zi−1)≤CgateI(U;Z_{i}\mid Z^{i-1})\leq C_{\mathrm{gate}}, and summing over i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m gives I⁡(U,Zm)≤m​CgateI(U;Z^{m})\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}}. ∎

Corollary III.2 (BSC(ε)(\varepsilon) bit-flip specialization).

Under Definition II.1, the conditional-capacity bound (12) holds with Cgate=1−h2​(ε)C_{\mathrm{gate}}=1-h_{2}\!\left(\varepsilon\right). Hence

I⁡(Rtn,X^t)≤I⁡(Rtn,Zm)≤m​Cgate.I(R_{t}^{n};\hat{X}_{t})\ \leq\ I(R_{t}^{n};Z^{m})\ \leq\ mC_{\mathrm{gate}}. (16)
Proof.

Immediate from Lemma III.1 with U=RtnU=R_{t}^{n}. ∎

Lemma III.3 (Compute information bound with a bb-bit reliable bypass).

Consider the GPU substrate model in Definition II.1, but allow the receiver to additionally generate an auxiliary variable VtV_{t} through a reliable path as an arbitrary (possibly randomized) function of RtnR_{t}^{n}, where H⁡(Vt)≤bH(V_{t})\leq b bits. If the receiver output has the form X^t=g⁡(Zm,Vt)\hat{X}_{t}=g(Z^{m},V_{t}) for some measurable function gg, then

I⁡(Rtn,X^t)≤b+m​Cgate.I(R_{t}^{n};\hat{X}_{t})\leq b+mC_{\mathrm{gate}}. (17)
Proof.

By data processing, I⁡(Rtn,X^t)≤I⁡(Rtn,Zm,Vt)I(R_{t}^{n};\hat{X}_{t})\leq I(R_{t}^{n};Z^{m},V_{t}). Applying the chain rule,

I⁡(Rtn,Zm,Vt)\displaystyle I(R_{t}^{n};Z^{m},V_{t}) =I⁡(Rtn,Zm)+I⁡(Rtn;Vt∣Zm)≤m​Cgate+H⁡(Vt)≤m​Cgate+b,\displaystyle=I(R_{t}^{n};Z^{m})+I(R_{t}^{n};V_{t}\mid Z^{m})\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}}+H(V_{t})\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}}+b, (18)

where I⁡(Rtn,Zm)≤m​CgateI(R_{t}^{n};Z^{m})\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}} follows from Lemma III.1 and I⁡(Rtn;Vt∣Zm)≤H⁡(Vt)≤bI(R_{t}^{n};V_{t}\mid Z^{m})\leq H(V_{t})\leq b. ∎

III-B Supply–Demand Converse for Task Distortion

Our main converses compare a task demand function, RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D), against a supply limited by communication and computation. To do so rigorously for block codes (which may couple many task instances), we will use the following standard “rate–distortion lower bound”: any reconstruction meeting an average distortion constraint must induce at least RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D) bits/sample of mutual information between YTY^{T} and X^T\hat{X}^{T}.

Lemma III.4 (Indirect rate–distortion lower bound on block mutual information).

Under the standing assumptions in Subsection II-D, let X^T\hat{X}^{T} be any (possibly stochastic) reconstruction of XTX^{T} based on YTY^{T}. If

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\big[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})\big]\leq D, (19)

then

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≥RX|Y​(D).\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \geq\ R_{X|Y}(D). (20)
Proof.

Define the per-instance distortions Dt≜𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]D_{t}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})]. Using the chain rule and noting that X^t\hat{X}_{t} is a component of X^T\hat{X}^{T},

I⁡(YT,X^T)\displaystyle I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T}) =∑t=1TI⁡(Yt;X^T∣Yt−1)≥∑t=1TI⁡(Yt;X^t∣Yt−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(Y_{t};\hat{X}^{T}\mid Y^{t-1})\geq\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(Y_{t};\hat{X}_{t}\mid Y^{t-1}) (21)
=∑t=1T(I⁡(Yt,X^t,Yt−1)−I⁡(Yt,Yt−1))=∑t=1TI⁡(Yt,X^t,Yt−1)≥∑t=1TI⁡(Yt,X^t),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(I(Y_{t};\hat{X}_{t},Y^{t-1})-I(Y_{t};Y^{t-1})\big)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(Y_{t};\hat{X}_{t},Y^{t-1})\geq\sum_{t=1}^{T}I(Y_{t};\hat{X}_{t}),

where I⁡(Yt,Yt−1)=0I(Y_{t};Y^{t-1})=0 since {Yt}t=1T\{Y_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} are i.i.d., and adding variables cannot decrease mutual information.

For each tt, the joint law of (Yt,X^t)(Y_{t},\hat{X}_{t}) induces a conditional distribution PX^t|YtP_{\hat{X}_{t}\mid Y_{t}} that attains distortion DtD_{t}. By the definition of RX|Y​(⋅)R_{X|Y}(\cdot) in (9), this implies

I⁡(Yt,X^t)≥RX|Y​(Dt)for every ​t.I(Y_{t};\hat{X}_{t})\geq R_{X|Y}(D_{t})\qquad\text{for every }t. (22)

Finally, RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D) is convex and nonincreasing in DD (as a rate–distortion function; see [19, 18]), so Jensen’s inequality gives

1T​∑t=1TRX|Y​(Dt)≥RX|Y​(1T​∑t=1TDt)≥RX|Y​(D).\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}R_{X|Y}(D_{t})\geq R_{X|Y}\Big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{t}\Big)\geq R_{X|Y}(D). (23)

Combining with (21) and dividing by TT yields (20). ∎

Define the per-instance information supply for task-direct processing as

Rsup≜min⁡{n​Cch,m​Cgate}bits/sample.R_{\mathrm{sup}}\triangleq\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ mC_{\mathrm{gate}}\}\quad\text{bits/sample}. (24)

We will repeatedly invoke Lemma III.1 by choosing the output variable to be an intermediate interface variable, thereby bounding the mutual information crossing that interface by the corresponding primitive budget times CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}}.

Theorem III.5 (Supply–demand converse).

Assume (S1)–(S3) in Subsection II-D, and consider the task-direct architecture in (10). If there exists an encoding and noisy-compute decoding scheme such that the (block) average distortion satisfies

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\big[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})\big]\leq D,

then

RX|Y​(D)≤Rsup=min⁡{n​Cch,m​Cgate}.R_{X|Y}(D)\ \leq\ R_{\mathrm{sup}}\;=\;\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ mC_{\mathrm{gate}}\}. (25)
Proof.

Let the overall TT-block scheme induce the joint law of (XT,YT,X^T)(X^{T},Y^{T},\hat{X}^{T}). By Lemma III.4, achieving average distortion at most DD implies

RX|Y​(D)≤1T​I​(YT,X^T).R_{X|Y}(D)\ \leq\ \frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T}). (26)

We now upper bound 1T​I​(YT,X^T)\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T}) by two cuts.

(Communication cut) Since YT→Sn​T→Rn​T→X^TY^{T}\to S^{nT}\to R^{nT}\to\hat{X}^{T}, data processing gives

I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(Sn​T,Rn​T).I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(S^{nT};R^{nT}).

By the standard memoryless-channel converse argument under the imposed input constraint,

I⁡(Sn​T,Rn​T)≤n​T​Cch,I(S^{nT};R^{nT})\leq nT\,C_{\mathrm{ch}},

and hence 1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤n​Cch\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq nC_{\mathrm{ch}}.

(Computation cut) Let ULU^{L} and ZLZ^{L} denote the intended and retrieved bits over the L=m​TL=mT vulnerable materializations. Under the no-bypass (commitment) assumption in Definition II.1, X^T\hat{X}^{T} is a (measurable) function of ZLZ^{L}, so Rn​T→ZL→X^TR^{nT}\to Z^{L}\to\hat{X}^{T} is a Markov chain and therefore

I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(Rn​T,X^T)≤I⁡(Rn​T,ZL).I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(R^{nT};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(R^{nT};Z^{L}).

Applying Lemma III.1 to the L=m​TL=mT primitive uses over the block gives I⁡(Rn​T,ZL)≤m​T​Cgate=L​CgateI(R^{nT};Z^{L})\leq mT\,C_{\mathrm{gate}}=L\,C_{\mathrm{gate}}, and hence 1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤m​Cgate\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}}.

Combining these two cuts with (26) yields (25). ∎

Interpretation. Theorem III.5 says that task performance is governed by the smaller of the physical channel supply n​CchnC_{\mathrm{ch}} and the receiver compute supply m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}}: when n​Cch≤m​CgatenC_{\mathrm{ch}}\leq mC_{\mathrm{gate}}, the benchmark reduces to the classical channel-limited remote rate–distortion constraint, whereas when m​Cgate≤n​CchmC_{\mathrm{gate}}\leq nC_{\mathrm{ch}}, unreliable computation becomes the active bottleneck and hard-separation can further reduce the usable compute supply to m2​Cgate\tfrac{m}{2}C_{\mathrm{gate}} (Corollary IV.22), yielding a strict separation loss under Corollary IV.23.

As a plug-in variation of the same task-direct converse, an explicit reliable side path simply adds its protected entropy budget to the compute cut.

Corollary III.6 (Supply–demand converse with a bb-bit reliable bypass).

Assume the setting of Theorem III.5, but replace the no-bypass compute model in Definition II.1 by the bb-bit bypass extension in Remark II.3. Then any scheme achieving average distortion at most DD must satisfy

RX|Y​(D)≤Rsup(b)≜min⁡{n​Cch,b+m​Cgate}.R_{X|Y}(D)\leq R_{\mathrm{sup}}^{(b)}\triangleq\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ b+mC_{\mathrm{gate}}\}. (27)

In particular, the baseline converse bound in Theorem III.5 is recovered by setting b=0b=0.

Proof.

The indirect rate–distortion lower bound and the communication cut are unchanged from Theorem III.5. Under the bb-bit bypass extension,

I⁡(Rn​T,X^T)≤I⁡(Rn​T,Zm​T,VT)≤m​T​Cgate+b​T,I(R^{nT};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(R^{nT};Z^{mT},V^{T})\leq mTC_{\mathrm{gate}}+bT,

so combining with Lemma III.4 yields (27). ∎

Supplementary plug-ins and task variants

Additional heterogeneous/word-level compute-supply replacements and a Fano-style classification benchmark are recorded in Appendix F.

III-C Achievability Under a Protected-Support Closure

Theorem III.5 also admits a Shannon-style achievability construction built from remote source coding, capacity-approaching channel coding, and internal coding across the memoryless compute primitive. The closure used by these forward statements is formalized next, and the internal-coding ingredient is recorded abstractly here and explicitly in Subsection F-E.

Scope note for achievability statements

The converse results in Sections III–IV use the committed/no-bypass closure, whereas the achievability statements below adopt the stronger protected-support closure of Assumption III.7; the forward and converse results therefore apply to different closures.

Standing regularity assumptions

Throughout the paper, source and reconstruction alphabets are understood as standard Borel spaces, the distortion measure is measurable and integrable under the relevant test channels and code-induced laws, and the indirect rate–distortion function is taken to be well defined under these standing conditions. We do not dwell further on these standard regularity assumptions.

Assumption III.7 (Protected-support closure for achievability).

The achievability statements are stated under the following stronger model-closure assumptions.

  1. (A1)

    Budgeted memoryless primitive accounting. Receiver-side vulnerability is captured by at most L=m​TL=mT uses of a DMC compute primitive WZ|UW_{Z|U} with capacity CgateC_{\mathrm{gate}} (Definition II.1), independent across uses given their inputs.

  2. (A2)

    Protected decoder/control support. The control, addressing, stagewise recoding, codebook lookup, and decoder/post-processing support machinery invoked in the achievability proofs is assumed reliable, or equivalently is implemented within a protected “reliable island” whose resource cost is not charged to the vulnerable-materialization budget mm. This stronger closure supports the Shannon-style achievability theorems stated here; if the same bookkeeping and recoding support must also be implemented on the vulnerable substrate and charged to mm, then Section V provides the stricter conservative model.

  3. (A3)

    Shannon-theoretic coding availability. The physical channel admits capacity-approaching codes of rate up to n​CchnC_{\mathrm{ch}} bits/sample with vanishing block error probability, and, more generally, for any allocated sub-budget m′≥0m^{\prime}\geq 0, the compute primitive admits internal redundancy codes of rate up to m′​Cgatem^{\prime}C_{\mathrm{gate}} bits/sample with vanishing block error probability (Proposition F.5). Likewise, by Proposition II.5, for any DD and any R>RX|Y​(D)R>R_{X|Y}(D), fixed-length indirect rate–distortion codes of rate RR exist in the Shannon asymptotic.

Table III summarizes the assumption and closure scope of representative results in the paper, making explicit the converse/achievability split across closures.

Theorem III.8 (Task-direct achievability under the protected-support closure).

Assume Assumption III.7. Then, for any distortion level DD such that

RX|Y​(D)<Rsup,R_{X|Y}(D)\;<\;R_{\mathrm{sup}}, (28)

there exists a task-direct scheme (Architecture (A)) whose average distortion satisfies 1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})]\leq D in the Shannon asymptotic regime (T→∞T\to\infty).

Mean-squared error (MSE)/unbounded-distortion note

Under squared-error distortion and finite second moment, Lemma J.1 closes the unbounded-distortion case; see Appendix J.

Proof.

Fix any rate RR such that RX|Y​(D)<R<RsupR_{X|Y}(D)<R<R_{\mathrm{sup}}. For each task-blocklength TT, let MT≜2⌊T​R⌋M_{T}\triangleq 2^{\lfloor TR\rfloor}.

(Remote source coding) By Proposition II.5, there exists a sequence of fixed-length indirect rate–distortion codes

(fT,ψT):𝒴T→{1,…,MT}→𝒳^T(f_{T},\psi_{T}):\ \mathcal{Y}^{T}\to\{1,\dots,M_{T}\}\to\hat{\mathcal{X}}^{T}

whose induced reconstruction X^RDT≜ψT​(fT​(YT))\hat{X}_{\mathrm{RD}}^{T}\triangleq\psi_{T}(f_{T}(Y^{T})) satisfies

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^RD,t)]≤D+ξT,ξT→0​as ​T→∞.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\big[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{\mathrm{RD},t})\big]\leq D+\xi_{T},\qquad\xi_{T}\to 0\ \text{as }T\to\infty. (29)

Let W≜fT​(YT)∈{1,…,MT}W\triangleq f_{T}(Y^{T})\in\{1,\dots,M_{T}\} denote the remote description index.

(Physical channel coding) Since log2⁡MT≤T​R\log_{2}M_{T}\leq TR and R<n​CchR<nC_{\mathrm{ch}}, Shannon’s channel coding theorem implies that there exists a sequence of length-n​TnT channel codes with a (reliable) decoder (e.g., implemented on a protected control plane as in Assumption III.7-(A2)) producing an estimate W~\tilde{W} from Rn​TR^{nT} such that

ϵch(T)≜ℙ⁡(W~≠W)⟶ 0as ​T→∞.\epsilon_{\mathrm{ch}}^{(T)}\triangleq\mathbb{P}(\tilde{W}\neq W)\ \longrightarrow\ 0\qquad\text{as }T\to\infty. (30)

(Internal compute-side redundancy) Since log2⁡MT≤T​R\log_{2}M_{T}\leq TR and R<m​CgateR<mC_{\mathrm{gate}}, Proposition F.5 guarantees the existence of a sequence of internal codes (encoder αT\alpha_{T} and decoder βT\beta_{T}) over the L=m​TL=mT primitive uses such that, if the receiver materializes UL=αT​(W~)U^{L}=\alpha_{T}(\tilde{W}) through the primitive to obtain ZLZ^{L} and forms W^≜βT​(ZL)\hat{W}\triangleq\beta_{T}(Z^{L}), then

ϵcomp(T)≜ℙ⁡(W^≠W~)⟶ 0as ​T→∞.\epsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}^{(T)}\triangleq\mathbb{P}(\hat{W}\neq\tilde{W})\ \longrightarrow\ 0\qquad\text{as }T\to\infty. (31)

(See Appendix H for a concrete correcting-network instantiation.)

(Overall task-direct receiver) The receiver algorithm is: decode W~\tilde{W} from Rn​TR^{nT}; materialize UL=αT​(W~)U^{L}=\alpha_{T}(\tilde{W}) through the L=m​TL=mT primitive uses; decode W^=βT​(ZL)\hat{W}=\beta_{T}(Z^{L}); and form the preliminary reconstruction X~T≜ψT​(W^)\tilde{X}^{T}\triangleq\psi_{T}(\hat{W}). We set X^T≜X~T\hat{X}^{T}\triangleq\tilde{X}^{T} as the final receiver output. This is a valid task-direct scheme of the form (10), since the final output depends on Rn​TR^{nT} only through the chosen materializations and the resulting ZLZ^{L}.

Let 𝖤T≜{W^≠W}\mathsf{E}_{T}\triangleq\{\hat{W}\neq W\}. By construction, 𝖤T⊆{W~≠W}∪{W^≠W~}\mathsf{E}_{T}\subseteq\{\tilde{W}\neq W\}\cup\{\hat{W}\neq\tilde{W}\}, hence by a union bound,

ℙ⁡(𝖤T)≤ϵch(T)+ϵcomp(T).\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{E}_{T})\ \leq\ \epsilon_{\mathrm{ch}}^{(T)}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}^{(T)}. (32)

On the event 𝖤Tc\mathsf{E}_{T}^{c}, we have W^=W\hat{W}=W and therefore X~T=ψT​(W)=X^RDT\tilde{X}^{T}=\psi_{T}(W)=\hat{X}_{\mathrm{RD}}^{T}.

If the distortion measure is bounded, 0≤d⁡(X,X^)≤dmax0\leq d(X,\hat{X})\leq d_{\max} almost surely, then combining (29) and (32) yields

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})] ≤(D+ξT)​ℙ​(𝖤Tc)+dmax​ℙ​(𝖤T)\displaystyle\leq(D+\xi_{T})\,\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{E}_{T}^{c})+d_{\max}\,\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{E}_{T}) (33)
≤D+ξT+dmax​(ϵch(T)+ϵcomp(T)).\displaystyle\leq D+\xi_{T}+d_{\max}\big(\epsilon_{\mathrm{ch}}^{(T)}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}^{(T)}\big). (34)

Letting T→∞T\to\infty gives the claimed achievability of DD.

For squared-error distortion with 𝔼⁡[X2]<∞\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]<\infty, apply Lemma J.1 with error event 𝖤T\mathsf{E}_{T} and (32); this closes mean-MSE achievability of DD. ∎

IV Architecture-Induced First-Order Compute Cuts Under Committed Interfaces

We first develop the two-stage and serial hard-separation specializations before stating the general receiver-internal compute min-cut converse in Subsection IV-C; Proposition IV.19 then records the no-tax soft-interface relaxation.

IV-A Two-Stage Hard-Separation Specialization: Interface Tax

Recall the hard-separation constraint in Definition II.6. In hard-separation, channel decoding is itself computed on the noisy substrate and its output is forced through an intermediate committed digital interface before task inference, creating the two serial mutual-information cuts formalized below. For a TT-block scheme, this induces the Markov chain

YT→Sn​T→Rn​T→B^T→X^T,Y^{T}\to S^{nT}\to R^{nT}\to\hat{B}^{T}\to\hat{X}^{T}, (35)

where B^T\hat{B}^{T} is the decoded (digital) representation and X^T\hat{X}^{T} is the task output.

We model the decoder stage as using at most mdec​Tm_{\mathrm{dec}}T unreliable primitives to map Rn​T↦B^TR^{nT}\mapsto\hat{B}^{T}, and the downstream task stage as using at most mtask​Tm_{\mathrm{task}}T unreliable primitives to map B^T↦X^T\hat{B}^{T}\mapsto\hat{X}^{T}, with mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m.

Lemma IV.1 (Information bound for each stage).

Under the TT-block hard-separation architecture (35),

I⁡(Rn​T,B^T)≤mdec​T​Cgate,I⁡(B^T,X^T)≤mtask​T​Cgate.I(R^{nT};\hat{B}^{T})\leq m_{\mathrm{dec}}T\,C_{\mathrm{gate}},\qquad I(\hat{B}^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq m_{\mathrm{task}}T\,C_{\mathrm{gate}}. (36)
Proof.

Each inequality follows by applying Lemma III.1 to the corresponding stage-specific bit-materialization process over the full block of length TT. ∎

Theorem IV.2 (Two-stage hard-separation converse with interface-tax specialization).

Under the TT-block hard-separation architecture (35), any scheme satisfies

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤min⁡{n​Cch,mdec​Cgate,mtask​Cgate}.\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \leq\ \min\big\{\,nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{\mathrm{dec}}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ m_{\mathrm{task}}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\big\}. (37)

Consequently,

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤min⁡{n​Cch,m2​Cgate}\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\,nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ \frac{m}{2}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\Big\} (38)

under the optimal budget split mdec=mtask=m2m_{\mathrm{dec}}=m_{\mathrm{task}}=\frac{m}{2}.

Proof.

The communication cut gives I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(Sn​T,Rn​T)≤n​T​CchI(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(S^{nT};R^{nT})\leq nTC_{\mathrm{ch}}. Under hard-separation (35), we have the Markov chain YT→Rn​T→B^T→X^TY^{T}\to R^{nT}\to\hat{B}^{T}\to\hat{X}^{T}, so I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(YT,B^T)≤I⁡(Rn​T,B^T)I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(Y^{T};\hat{B}^{T})\leq I(R^{nT};\hat{B}^{T}) and also I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(B^T,X^T)I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(\hat{B}^{T};\hat{X}^{T}) by data processing. Applying Lemma IV.1 yields (37). Maximizing the minimum of (mdec,mtask)(m_{\mathrm{dec}},m_{\mathrm{task}}) subject to mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m gives m/2m/2, yielding (38). ∎

Remark IV.3 (Committed-interface tax versus classical receiver models).

Theorem IV.2 is not a failure of Shannon source–channel separation: with reliable receiver processing, an intermediate digital description can be made asymptotically error-free and does not create an additional first-order bottleneck [1, 18]. The additional penalty studied here arises only when task-relevant information must cross a receiver-internal committed vulnerable interface under an explicit compute budget; classical appended noisy-receiver/additional-noise models do not create such an internal cut [23, 24, 25]. Letting m→∞m\to\infty only makes the compute-side cut nonbinding; it does not by itself recover the classical noisy-receiver/additional-noise closure. In the special case with no communication bottleneck and exact-function recovery, the compute-supply term m​CgatemC_{\mathrm{gate}} may also be read as a converse-side ceiling analogous to Simon’s computation capacity [14], but our setting keeps an explicit communication cut and indirect-distortion demand. Equation (38) is therefore a structural hard-separation effect.

Theorem IV.4 (Two-stage achievability under the protected-support closure).

Assume the conditions of Theorem III.8 and fix any split mdec,mtask≥0m_{\mathrm{dec}},m_{\mathrm{task}}\geq 0 with mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m. Then, for any distortion level DD such that

RX|Y​(D)<min⁡{n​Cch,mdec​Cgate,mtask​Cgate},R_{X|Y}(D)\ <\ \min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{\mathrm{dec}}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ m_{\mathrm{task}}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\}, (39)

there exists a two-stage construction under Assumption III.7 whose average distortion satisfies 1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})]\leq D in the Shannon asymptotic regime (T→∞T\to\infty).

Proof.

Use the achievability template of Theorem III.8. Choose

RX|Y​(D)<R<min⁡{n​Cch,mdec​Cgate,mtask​Cgate},R_{X|Y}(D)<R<\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{\mathrm{dec}}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ m_{\mathrm{task}}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\},

and let WW be the common remote-description index, reliably decoded from the physical channel as W~\tilde{W}. Since R<mdec​CgateR<m_{\mathrm{dec}}C_{\mathrm{gate}} and R<mtask​CgateR<m_{\mathrm{task}}C_{\mathrm{gate}}, Proposition F.5 yields two internal codes over the stage-11 and stage-22 primitive budgets, producing a committed interface B^T≡W^dec\hat{B}^{T}\equiv\hat{W}_{\mathrm{dec}} and final index W^task\hat{W}_{\mathrm{task}} with vanishing stage errors. A union bound gives ℙ⁡(W^task≠W)→0\mathbb{P}(\hat{W}_{\mathrm{task}}\neq W)\to 0, so on the success event X^T=ψT​(W^task)=X^RDT\hat{X}^{T}=\psi_{T}(\hat{W}_{\mathrm{task}})=\hat{X}_{\mathrm{RD}}^{T}. The bounded-distortion case then follows exactly as in Theorem III.8, and the squared-error case follows from Lemma J.1. ∎

IV-B Serial KK-Stage Extensions

We now extend the two-stage hard-separation converse to serial KK-stage pipelines, where each additional committed interface creates another compute cut.

Practical receivers often contain multiple serial digital interfaces beyond the basic “decode–then–task” split. Examples include pipelines of the form decode →\rightarrow decrypt →\rightarrow decompress →\rightarrow infer, or multi-module baseband stacks in which intermediate representations are stored and reloaded across the memory hierarchy. On an unreliable substrate, each such serial interface can become a mandatory information bottleneck.

We capture this phenomenon by considering a KK-stage serial organization with intermediate interfaces U1,…,UK−1U_{1},\dots,U_{K-1}. For a TT-block scheme, let U0≜Rn​TU_{0}\triangleq R^{nT} denote the channel output block and UK≜X^TU_{K}\triangleq\hat{X}^{T} denote the final task-output block. Stage k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\} maps Uk−1U_{k-1} to UkU_{k} using at most mk​Tm_{k}T unreliable primitives (bit materializations), with a total budget ∑k=1Kmk≤m\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}\leq m.

Theorem IV.5 (Serial KK-stage compute-cut converse).

Consider any receiver architecture that induces the Markov chain

YT→Sn​T→U0(=Rn​T)→U1→⋯→UK−1→UK(=X^T),Y^{T}\to S^{nT}\to U_{0}(=R^{nT})\to U_{1}\to\cdots\to U_{K-1}\to U_{K}(=\hat{X}^{T}), (40)

and suppose each stage Uk−1→UkU_{k-1}\to U_{k} is implemented on the noisy-computation substrate using at most mk​Tm_{k}T unreliable primitives. Then

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤min⁡{n​Cch,m1​Cgate,m2​Cgate,…,mK​Cgate}.\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\,nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{1}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ m_{2}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ \dots,\ m_{K}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\Big\}. (41)

In particular, under a fixed total compute budget ∑k=1Kmk≤m\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}\leq m, the right-hand side is maximized by equal splitting mk=m/Km_{k}=m/K and yields the simplified bound

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤min⁡{n​Cch,mK​Cgate}.\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\,nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ \frac{m}{K}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\Big\}. (42)
Proof.

The communication cut gives I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(Sn​T,Rn​T)≤n​T​CchI(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq I(S^{nT};R^{nT})\leq nTC_{\mathrm{ch}}. Moreover, for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, the Markov chains YT→Uk→X^TY^{T}\to U_{k}\to\hat{X}^{T} and YT→Uk−1→UkY^{T}\to U_{k-1}\to U_{k} imply, by data processing, that

I⁡(YT,X^T)≤I⁡(YT,Uk)≤I⁡(Uk−1,Uk).I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\ \leq\ I(Y^{T};U_{k})\ \leq\ I(U_{k-1};U_{k}). (43)

Applying Lemma III.1 to each stage over the full block (with input Uk−1U_{k-1} and output UkU_{k}) yields I⁡(Uk−1,Uk)≤mk​T​CgateI(U_{k-1};U_{k})\leq m_{k}TC_{\mathrm{gate}}. Taking the minimum over k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K yields (41). Finally, maximizing mink⁡mk\min_{k}m_{k} subject to ∑kmk≤m\sum_{k}m_{k}\leq m is achieved by equal splitting, yielding (42). ∎

Corollary IV.6 (Serial KK-stage achievability under the protected-support closure).

Assume the conditions of Theorem III.8. Fix stage budgets m1,…,mK≥0m_{1},\dots,m_{K}\geq 0 with

∑k=1Kmk≤m.\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}\leq m.

Then, for any distortion level DD such that

RX|Y​(D)<min⁡{n​Cch,m1​Cgate,…,mK​Cgate},R_{X|Y}(D)\ <\ \min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{1}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ \dots,\ m_{K}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\}, (44)

there exists a serial KK-stage construction under Assumption III.7 whose average distortion satisfies 1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[d⁡(Xt,X^t)]≤D\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d(X_{t},\hat{X}_{t})]\leq D in the Shannon asymptotic regime (T→∞T\to\infty). In particular, under equal splitting mk=m/Km_{k}=m/K, any DD satisfying

RX|Y​(D)<min⁡{n​Cch,(m/K)​Cgate}R_{X|Y}(D)<\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ (m/K)C_{\mathrm{gate}}\}

is achievable under Assumption III.7.

Proof.

Repeat the common-index construction of Theorem IV.4, replacing the two vulnerable rematerialization stages by KK stages with budgets m1​T,…,mK​Tm_{1}T,\dots,m_{K}T. For any

RX|Y​(D)<R<min⁡{n​Cch,m1​Cgate,…,mK​Cgate},R_{X|Y}(D)<R<\min\{nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ m_{1}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ \dots,\ m_{K}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\},

the physical channel decodes the common index reliably, and Proposition F.5 yields stagewise internal codes for all KK vulnerable stages. A union bound gives vanishing overall index error, so the bounded-distortion and squared-error conclusions follow exactly as in Theorem III.8. The equal-splitting specialization is immediate. ∎

IV-C General DAG Receiver-Internal Compute Min-Cut Theorem

Theorem IV.5 covers purely serial organizations. We now move to a specified DAG interface decomposition of the receiver computation, where each s𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}}–t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} cut becomes a candidate compute bottleneck.

The serial model of Subsection IV-B captures pipelines in which task-relevant information must traverse a single path of committed digital interfaces. Many practical receiver stacks, however, contain parallel branches (e.g., multi-thread baseband processing, cached side information, or architectural “skip” connections) so that information can traverse multiple interface paths. The next theorem extends the same interface-based bound to general receiver computation graphs.

Consider a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G=(𝒱,ℰ)G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) with a designated source node s𝒢∈𝒱s_{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathcal{V} and sink node t𝒢∈𝒱t_{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathcal{V}. Over a task block of length TT, node s𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}} holds the channel output block Us𝒢≜Rn​TU_{s_{\mathcal{G}}}\triangleq R^{nT} and node t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} outputs the final task block Ut𝒢≜X^TU_{t_{\mathcal{G}}}\triangleq\hat{X}^{T}. Each edge e=(u,v)∈ℰe=(u,v)\in\mathcal{E} represents a committed interface variable WeW_{e} that is generated from the tail-node state UuU_{u} on the noisy substrate using at most me​Tm_{e}T unreliable primitives, and is then available to the head node vv.22 2 Feedback and iterative processing can be accommodated by unfolding iterations into a larger DAG over time; the same cut-set argument then applies to the unfolded graph. We assume that the induced joint law is consistent with this DAG in the sense that all downstream computations depend on Rn​TR^{nT} only through the collection of committed interface variables {We}e∈ℰ\{W_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}.

Definition IV.7 (DAG interface representation).

A TT-block receiver scheme is said to admit a DAG interface representation on G=(𝒱,ℰ)G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) with source s𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}} and sink t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} if there exist node-state random variables {Uv}v∈𝒱\{U_{v}\}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}, committed interface variables {We}e∈ℰ\{W_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}, node-private randomness variables {ζv}v≠s𝒢\{\zeta_{v}\}_{v\neq s_{\mathcal{G}}}, and for each edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) an edge-private randomness variable ξe\xi_{e}, fresh primitive-noise variables Ne,1,…,Ne,MeN_{e,1},\dots,N_{e,M_{e}}, and a deterministic integer Me≤me​TM_{e}\leq m_{e}T, such that Us𝒢=Rn​TU_{s_{\mathcal{G}}}=R^{nT} and Ut𝒢=X^TU_{t_{\mathcal{G}}}=\hat{X}^{T}, and for every node v≠s𝒢v\neq s_{\mathcal{G}},

Uv=gv​(WIn⁡(v),ζv),U_{v}=g_{v}\!\big(W_{\mathrm{In}(v)},\,\zeta_{v}\big),

where WIn⁡(v)≜{We:e=(u,v)∈ℰ}W_{\mathrm{In}(v)}\triangleq\{W_{e}:e=(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}\} are the incoming interface variables. Moreover, for each edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) there is an edge-local noisy subroutine of length MeM_{e} with transcript ZeMe≜(Ze,1,…,Ze,Me)Z_{e}^{M_{e}}\triangleq(Z_{e,1},\dots,Z_{e,M_{e}}) such that

Ae,i=αe,i(Uu,Zei−1,ξe),Ze,i∼WZ|U(⋅∣Ae,i),i=1,…,Me,A_{e,i}=\alpha_{e,i}\!\big(U_{u},Z_{e}^{i-1},\xi_{e}\big),\qquad Z_{e,i}\sim W_{Z|U}(\cdot\mid A_{e,i}),\qquad i=1,\dots,M_{e},

and

We=βe​(ZeMe,ξe).W_{e}=\beta_{e}\!\big(Z_{e}^{M_{e}},\xi_{e}\big).

The variables Ne,1,…,Ne,MeN_{e,1},\dots,N_{e,M_{e}} are the fresh primitive noises that realize the conditional draws Ze,i∼WZ|U(⋅∣Ae,i)Z_{e,i}\sim W_{Z|U}(\cdot\mid A_{e,i}). Equivalently, there exists a measurable function ϕ\phi such that

Ze,i=ϕ⁡(Ae,i,Ne,i),Z_{e,i}=\phi(A_{e,i},N_{e,i}),

where the distribution of Ne,iN_{e,i} is chosen so that Ze,i∣Ae,i=a∼WZ|U(⋅∣a)Z_{e,i}\mid A_{e,i}=a\sim W_{Z|U}(\cdot\mid a). The variable WeW_{e} is the only information from uu made available to the head node vv. Moreover, the family

{ζv}v≠s𝒢∪{ξe}e∈ℰ∪{Ne,i:e∈ℰ, 1≤i≤Me}\{\zeta_{v}\}_{v\neq s_{\mathcal{G}}}\;\cup\;\{\xi_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\;\cup\;\{N_{e,i}:e\in\mathcal{E},\ 1\leq i\leq M_{e}\}

is mutually independent and jointly independent of the upstream variables (YT,Rn​T)(Y^{T},R^{nT}), reflecting the operational model in which these are fresh receiver-internal randomness variables generated independently of the source/channel realization.

The graph GG represents a specified interface decomposition of the receiver architecture. It does not assert that arbitrary node fusion or node splitting is free; such transformations are admissible only when the corresponding intermediate state is not treated as a committed vulnerable interface, or when its cost is accounted for elsewhere.

For a vertex subset Ω⊆𝒱\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{V}, define the outgoing edge boundary

∂+(Ω)≜{(u,v)∈ℰ:u∈Ω,v∈Ωc}.\partial^{+}(\Omega)\ \triangleq\ \big\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u\in\Omega,\ v\in\Omega^{c}\big\}. (45)
Lemma IV.8 (Cut-interface separation).

Under Definition IV.7, fix any cut Ω⊆𝒱\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{V} with s𝒢∈Ωs_{\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega and t𝒢∉Ωt_{\mathcal{G}}\notin\Omega, and let

W∂+(Ω)≜{We:e∈∂+(Ω)}.W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)}\triangleq\{W_{e}:e\in\partial^{+}(\Omega)\}.

Also define

EΩcint≜{(u,v)∈ℰ:u,v∈Ωc},E_{\Omega^{c}}^{\mathrm{int}}\triangleq\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u,v\in\Omega^{c}\},

and

SΩc≜({ζv:v∈Ωc},{ξe:e∈EΩcint},{Ne,i:e∈EΩcint, 1≤i≤Me}).S_{\Omega^{c}}\triangleq\Bigl(\{\zeta_{v}:v\in\Omega^{c}\},\{\xi_{e}:e\in E_{\Omega^{c}}^{\mathrm{int}}\},\{N_{e,i}:e\in E_{\Omega^{c}}^{\mathrm{int}},\ 1\leq i\leq M_{e}\}\Bigr).

Then the following two properties hold: (i) there exists a measurable function ψΩ\psi_{\Omega} such that

X^T=Ut𝒢=ψΩ​(W∂+(Ω),SΩc);\hat{X}^{T}=U_{t_{\mathcal{G}}}=\psi_{\Omega}\!\big(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\big);

(ii) SΩc⟂Rn​TS_{\Omega^{c}}\perp R^{nT}. Consequently,

I⁡(Rn​T,X^T)≤I⁡(Rn​T,W∂+(Ω),SΩc)=I⁡(Rn​T;W∂+(Ω)|SΩc).I(R^{nT};\hat{X}^{T})\;\leq\;I\!\big(R^{nT};W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\big)\;=\;I\!\big(R^{nT};W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)}\,\big|\,S_{\Omega^{c}}\big).
Proof.

Proof of (i). Because GG is acyclic, the nodes in Ωc\Omega^{c} can be ordered topologically as v1,…,vmv_{1},\dots,v_{m}. We claim by induction over this order that, for every r∈{1,…,m}r\in\{1,\dots,m\}, the node state UvrU_{v_{r}} and every interface variable WeW_{e} on an internal edge e=(vr,w)e=(v_{r},w) with w∈Ωcw\in\Omega^{c} are measurable functions of (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr).

For r=1r=1, every incoming edge to v1v_{1} either comes from Ω\Omega and therefore belongs to ∂+(Ω)\partial^{+}(\Omega), or does not exist. Hence

Uv1=gv1​(WIn⁡(v1),ζv1)U_{v_{1}}=g_{v_{1}}\!\big(W_{\mathrm{In}(v_{1})},\,\zeta_{v_{1}}\big)

is a measurable function of (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr). If e=(v1,w)e=(v_{1},w) is any edge with w∈Ωcw\in\Omega^{c}, then the edge-local recursion

Ae,i=αe,i​(Uv1,Zei−1,ξe),Ze,i=ϕ⁡(Ae,i,Ne,i),We=βe​(ZeMe,ξe)A_{e,i}=\alpha_{e,i}\!\big(U_{v_{1}},Z_{e}^{i-1},\xi_{e}\big),\qquad Z_{e,i}=\phi(A_{e,i},N_{e,i}),\qquad W_{e}=\beta_{e}\!\big(Z_{e}^{M_{e}},\xi_{e}\big)

shows that WeW_{e} is also a measurable function of (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr).

Assume the claim holds up to r−1r-1. Consider node vrv_{r}. Every incoming edge from Ω\Omega belongs to ∂+(Ω)\partial^{+}(\Omega), while every incoming edge from Ωc\Omega^{c} originates at one of v1,…,vr−1v_{1},\dots,v_{r-1}. By the induction hypothesis, all such internal incoming interface variables are measurable functions of (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr). Therefore

Uvr=gvr​(WIn⁡(vr),ζvr)U_{v_{r}}=g_{v_{r}}\!\big(W_{\mathrm{In}(v_{r})},\,\zeta_{v_{r}}\big)

is a measurable function of (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr). The same edge-local recursion then shows that every internal outgoing edge e=(vr,w)e=(v_{r},w) with w∈Ωcw\in\Omega^{c} has interface variable WeW_{e} measurable with respect to (W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\bigl(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\bigr). This completes the induction.

Since t𝒢∈Ωct_{\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega^{c}, we obtain

X^T=Ut𝒢=ψΩ​(W∂+(Ω),SΩc)\hat{X}^{T}=U_{t_{\mathcal{G}}}=\psi_{\Omega}\!\big(W_{\partial^{+}(\Omega)},S_{\Omega^{c}}\big)

for some measurable function ψΩ\psi_{\Omega}.

Proof of (ii). Remark IV.11 (Serial chains and skip connections as special cases).

If GG is a serial chain with KK edges, every s𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}}–t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} cut crosses exactly one edge and (47) reduces to Theorem IV.5. Example IV.10 quantifies this depth-induced loss under a fixed total budget. More generally, adding a “skip” edge that carries side information from an earlier node to a later node creates parallel paths and can strictly increase the min-cut term in (47), thereby mitigating depth-induced bottlenecks. This provides an information-theoretic rationale for hybrid interfaces and architectural bypasses beyond the purely serial model.

Remark IV.12 (Heterogeneous primitives and reliable bypasses).

The cut-set term in (47) depends on the compute substrate only through per-use information bounds. If an interface edge ee is implemented using heterogeneous primitives with per-class budgets (me,1,…,me,J)(m_{e,1},\dots,m_{e,J}) per task instance, then the contribution of ee becomes ∑j=1Jme,j​Cgate(j)\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{e,j}C_{\mathrm{gate}}^{(j)} by Lemma F.1. Likewise, a bb-bit reliable bypass (Remark II.3) can be represented as an additional reliable edge of capacity bb (bits per task instance), which simply adds to the corresponding cut capacity and recovers the bypass relaxation in Corollary III.6.

Compute supply as a min-cut of the receiver computation graph. Theorem IV.9 also suggests a max–min allocation problem over interface budgets mem_{e}: equal splitting is optimal in serial architectures (Theorem IV.5), whereas multi-branch architectures can exploit parallel paths to relax depth-induced bottlenecks.

Remark IV.13 (Relation of Theorem IV.9 to classical network cut-sets).

Theorem IV.9 is formally cut-set-like, but its content differs from a classical communication-network cut-set in two respects. First, the cut edges are receiver-internal committed interfaces rather than external links with prescribed capacities, and each contribution me​Cgatem_{e}C_{\mathrm{gate}} is derived from Lemma III.1 for the noisy materialization of WeW_{e}, not postulated as an exogenous link throughput. Second, together with Lemma III.4, the theorem limits the task-relevant mutual information needed to attain distortion DD through RX|Y​(D)R_{X|Y}(D), rather than the rate of reliably communicating an independent message. The theorem thus turns committed materialization into induced compute cut values and couples those values to indirect rate–distortion demand.

IV-D Plug-Ins and Architectural Variants

Theorems IV.2, IV.5, and IV.9 remain the baseline references throughout this subsection: the variants below act only by changing the active cut or its effective capacity.

Corollary IV.14 (Hard-separation interface tax with a bb-bit reliable bypass).

Then any scheme satisfies

1T​I​(YT,X^T)≤min⁡{n​Cch,b+mdec​Cgate,b+mtask​Cgate}.\frac{1}{T}I(Y^{T};\hat{X}^{T})\leq\min\big\{\,nC_{\mathrm{ch}},\ b+m_{\mathrm{dec}}C_{\mathrm{gate}},\ b+m_{\mathrm{task}}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\big\}. (52)

Theorem IV.15 (Two-stage achievability with a protected bypass).

Assume the conditions of Theorem III.8. in the Shannon asymptotic regime (T→∞)(T\to\infty).

Under the total vulnerable-budget constraint mdec+mtask≤mm_{\mathrm{dec}}+m_{\mathrm{task}}\leq m, maximizing min⁡{mdec,mtask}\min\{m_{\mathrm{dec}},m_{\mathrm{task}}\} gives the symmetric split mdec=mtask=m/2m_{\mathrm{dec}}=m_{\mathrm{task}}=m/2, so every distortion level satisfying

is achievable under Assumption III.7. ∎
